name: Personas
obj: Turn research findings into a few evidence-based user profiles built on behaviours, needs and pain points.
who: CoDesign team clusters research and drafts personas · Client challenges them · Users or frontline staff can validate.
acc: CoDesign lead checks each trait against evidence.
inputs: Field findings, quotes, observations, data. Minimum evidence: each persona draws on at least 3 interviews or observations.
output: 2-4 personas: context, behaviours, goals, needs, motivations, pain points, quote, key journey moments, design implications.
std: Every trait links to evidence or is marked as an assumption.
mistakes: Demographic personas ('Sophie, 34, loves yoga') · invented quotes · too many personas.
example: HEAL: 'Ruth, the worried visitor' is defined by behaviour (visits at lunch, asks nurses whether Dad ate) and need (to know and help), not by age. Quote is from interview F02 [fictional dataset].
cred: Eli Lilly persona examples cited in S05 slide 25 ('Night-shift Marie') — confirm approved artifact.
prompt: 'From this interview synthesis [paste], propose 3 behaviour-based personas. For each trait cite the evidence ID or tag [ASSUMPTION]. No invented quotes.'
verify: Trait-to-evidence links; remove stereotypes and any quote not in transcripts.
fallback: Cluster stickies by behaviour on Miro, name each cluster with a verb phrase, fill the 11-field template.
l_obj: Rewrite a demographic persona into a behaviour-based one with evidence for each trait.
explain: A persona is discovered, not invented.

exercise.situation: Your team proposes: 'Sophie, 34, marketing manager, loves yoga and healthy food.'
questions: What is wrong with this persona?
Which evidence would you need to keep or drop each trait?
Rewrite it around a behaviour.

answer_key.sample_answer: It is demographic and unsourced; traits do not change design decisions. Rewrite: 'The 15-minute luncher: eats at her desk on meeting-heavy days, wants food she can trust without queuing.'
answer_key.success_criteria: Persona named by behaviour; each trait tagged evidence or assumption.

name: Journey Map
obj: Show the end-to-end experience across key moments, to understand what users do, think, feel and need, and where it breaks.
who: CoDesign team synthesises research, structures the journey and facilitates validation · Client/project team brings operational knowledge and challenges the map · Users and frontline staff provide the evidence and can validate key moments.
acc: CoDesign lead (N2+) signs off that every pain point carries evidence.
when: During Define, once personas and research findings exist. After or alongside 04.01, before How Might We questions and workshop challenges.
inputs: Personas; interview findings, observations, quotes; existing processes; touchpoints; Context Base; operational data. Minimum evidence: each stage supported by at least one observation or interview; each pain point by 2+ sources or marked [TO VALIDATE].
steps: Define the persona and the journey scope (start and end)
Identify 5-7 stages from the user's point of view
Map actions and touchpoints (physical, human, digital, printed)
Extract opportunity areas and How Might We questions
output: An evidence-based Journey Map: stages, actions, touchpoints, thoughts, emotions, needs, pain points, moments that matter, evidence and opportunities.
std: Readable by a non-attendee in 2 minutes; each pain point shows its evidence; 3-6 opportunity areas written as How Might We questions.
quality: Maps the real experience, not the ideal process; end-to-end; usable for decisions and co-creation.
mistakes: Mapping the operator's process ('service phase 2') · starting at the restaurant door instead of the decision to come · emotions without evidence · 15 stages · opportunities written as solutions.
handoff: Agreed map + top pain points + HMW questions → 04.03 Inspiration, 04.05 Pre-read and 05.04 Future Journey. Exploratory only: it does not decide solutions.
example: WORK, Northbridge (fictional): 7 stages from 'Decide to come in' to 'Leave'. Moment that matters 1: 'Lunch' — team splits in two queues (observed, median wait 11 min) and loses the shared moment. Moment that matters 2: 'Find a place to work' — 34% of service tickets are about quiet space. HMW: 'How might we make the team lunch a 20-minute moment instead of a 45-minute logistics task?'

var.PLAY: Dev's matchday: the valley is half-time (62% of kiosk sales in 9 minutes); journey starts at 'plan the day', ends at 'travel home'.
var.HEAL: Ruth and Arthur's meal journey: the pain is between ordering (24 h before) and delivery, not the food; family is invisible. Clinical sign-off needed for any change.
var.LEARN: Leila's campus day: the 3-hour gap is the valley; the journey starts at 'plan the day' and includes the car.

cred: OS Journey Map agent page lists Microsoft (6-stage hybrid worker), Roland-Garros (7-stage spectator) and Clariane (5-stage resident dining) as past outputs — source claims, artifacts to verify in SharePoint before showing.
tools: Miro journey widget, Figma templates, Illustrator A0 print
deck: [S03, slides 40-43] · [S05, slide 25] Eli Lilly journey (Arrival → food → workspace → break → departure)
prompt: Journey Map agent, Research-grounded mode: 'Persona: Maya, anchor-day coordinator (Northbridge, Corporate Services, North America). Journey type: daily journey, 7 stages. Layers: actions, thoughts, emotions, touchpoints, opportunities. Research data: [paste interview synthesis + observation notes]. Tag each row [EVIDENCE], [ASSUMPTION] or [TO VALIDATE]. No invented quotes. Output: stage table, emotion curve, top 5 pain points, 4-6 HMW opportunity zones.'
verify: Every [EVIDENCE] tag against the synthesis; stage names from the user's point of view; delete any verbatim not in the transcript; check the emotion curve has real highs and lows; decide which opportunities go to the workshop (human decision).
fallback: Draw the map on paper or Miro with stickies: columns = stages, rows = Actions / Touchpoints / Thoughts / Feelings / Pain points / Opportunities. Add a red dot on each pain point and write its source on the sticky.
l_obj: Given a persona and an evidence pack, build a 5-7 stage journey with at least 2 evidenced moments that matter and 3 How Might We questions.
explain: A journey map is a picture of what really happens to one person, over time, with proof. It is a decision tool, not decoration. Start where the user's experience starts (often before arrival) and stop where it really ends.

templates.label: Journey print template A0 (.ai, SharePoint 02_Define/02_Consumer Journeys)

exercise.situation: You are mapping the lunch journey of a hybrid worker on a corporate campus (Northbridge pack).
questions: Where does the journey really start and end?
Name two moments that matter and say why.
For one pain point, what evidence would you attach?

answer_key.sample_answer: Start: the evening before or morning decision to come in (the lunch plan starts there); end: back at the desk or leaving. Moments that matter: queue at 12:20 (observed, 11-min wait) and 'regroup at the table' (team lead quote). Evidence: observation log + interview P07 + service-desk ticket data. Weak answer: starts at 'enter restaurant', lists 'menu boring' with no source.
answer_key.success_criteria: Starts before the service touchpoint; 2 moments that matter each with a source; HMW is a question, not a solution.

name: Inspiration Idea Sheets
obj: Turn opportunity areas into tangible inspiration that widens thinking before the workshop, without prescribing solutions.
who: CoDesign team selects and designs the sheets · Experts suggest references.
acc: CoDesign lead checks each sheet links to a real need.
when: After the journey and opportunity areas, before the workshop.
inputs: Opportunity areas, benchmark principles, trends. Minimum evidence: each sheet cites its source example.
steps: Connect to needs and the journey
output: Inspiration Idea Sheets: example, principle, related need, 'What if…?' provocation.
std: One sheet = one principle + one 'What if…?' + source.
quality: Visual, concise, diverse, provocative, connected to insights.
mistakes: Sheets that are finished solutions · all examples from one sector · no link to the journey.
handoff: Sheets printed or on Miro for 05.06 and 05.04.
example: PLAY: sheet 'Move the wait' — airport fast-track principle; 'What if half-time food was ready before the whistle?' Linked to Dev's half-time valley.

var.WORK: 'Restaurant as team table' from co-working spaces.
var.HEAL: 'Room-service window' from hotels; check clinical fit.

prompt: 'For opportunity [HMW], create 3 inspiration sheets: 1 in-sector, 2 out-of-sector. Each: example + source, principle in one sentence, What if…? Do not propose a final solution.'
verify: Sources live; provocations open, not prescriptive.
fallback: Use benchmark principles; one A4 per principle with a photo, a sentence and a 'What if…?'.
l_obj: Write one principle and one 'What if…?' provocation from two examples.
explain: Inspiration opens the field of possibilities; it does not replace ideation.

templates.label: Project template root (SharePoint) — Inspiration sheet template: TO LOCATE, owner Gabriel

os_agents.name: Inspiration Sheets (OS lists it under Co-create)

exercise.situation: Opportunity area: 'make the last ten minutes of the break feel restful'.
questions: Find two inspirations, one inside and one outside the sector.
Write each key principle in one sentence.
Turn one into a 'What if…?' provocation.

answer_key.sample_answer: Principle example: 'Signal the end of a break gently so people stop checking the time.' What if…? 'What if the space told you when it was time to go?'
answer_key.success_criteria: Principle is transferable; provocation is open.

name: Concept Sheets
obj: Make 3-5 promising directions tangible enough to be challenged and enriched in the workshop.
who: CoDesign team drafts directions · Client experts challenge feasibility.
acc: CoDesign lead checks each concept traces to a need and lists assumptions.
when: Before the workshop, after opportunity areas.
inputs: Opportunity areas, personas, journey, inspiration. Minimum evidence: each concept cites a pain point.
output: Visual Concept Sheets: ambition, need, value, experience before/during/after, components, assumptions.
std: Each sheet lists its riskiest assumption.
mistakes: Presenting concepts as decided · no assumptions · concepts that ignore operations.
handoff: Define concept sheets are EXPLORATORY directions for the workshop. Participants' contributions are captured on 05.07 Idea Sheets; selected ideas are strengthened after the workshop in 06.X1 Concept Development.
example: WORK: 'Team Table' — book a table and pre-order as a team; riskiest assumption: teams will commit to a time the day before. [fictional]

var.HEAL: 'Choose closer to the meal' same-day ordering.

cred: Santander: '20 concept sheets' (S06 slide 4) — confirm artifacts before reuse.
prompt: 'Draft 3 concept directions for [HMW] for persona [x]. For each: one-line idea, need + evidence, before/during/after, components (space/service/people/ways of working/tech), riskiest assumption.'
verify: Need and evidence links; feasibility flags; remove anything presented as validated.
fallback: Fill the 12-field template by hand; sketch the 'during' moment.
l_obj: State the need, the before/during/after experience and the killer assumption of a concept.
explain: A Concept Sheet makes an idea tangible enough to challenge, not finished enough to prevent change.

templates.label: Project template root (SharePoint) — Concept sheet template: TO LOCATE, owner Gabriel

os_agents.name: Concept Sheets (OS lists it under Co-create)

exercise.situation: The team has an idea: 'an app that lets you pre-order your lunch'.
questions: Which need does it answer, and what is the evidence?
Describe before, during, after.
Which assumption would kill it if false?

answer_key.sample_answer: Need: save time at peak (observed queue). Killer assumption: people will decide what to eat before 11:00.
answer_key.success_criteria: Need is evidenced; killer assumption is testable.

name: Pre-read J-7
obj: Prepare participants one week before the workshop with the essential context, users and opportunities.
who: CoDesign team writes · Client sponsor sends or co-signs.
acc: CoDesign lead approves content; sponsor approves sharing and anonymisation.
when: Sent at D-7 (seven days before the workshop).
inputs: Journey highlights, personas, insights, opportunities, workshop objective. Minimum evidence: every finding is in the approved Define outputs.
output: A short pre-read (6-15 light slides or ≤10 pages) consumable in 10-15 minutes.
std: Reading time tested at ≤15 min by someone outside the project; no exercise answers or predetermined concepts revealed.
mistakes: Sending the full Discovery report · revealing the concepts the team prefers · no ask of participants.
handoff: Pre-read approved → 04.06 Mini Podcast script derives only from it.
example: HEAL: St Aldric pre-read — why we are here, Ruth and Arthur, the meal journey in one picture, 3 insights, 2 HMW questions, 'Bring one story of a meal that went well'. [fictional]

var.WORK: Northbridge: one-page journey with the lunch valley.

cred: Cooper pre-read is an internal working example; check sharing rules.
tools: Word/PowerPoint, Miro slide container 'PreRead_Template_CoDesign.pptx' on V1 board
prompt: No dedicated agent. Generic Claude prompt: 'From these approved Define outputs [paste], draft a 10-15 minute pre-read: Why → Ambition → What we learned → Personas → Journey highlights → Insights → Opportunities → Workshop objective → Preparation. Do not reveal exercise answers or concepts.'
verify: Every fact appears in approved outputs; anonymisation; reading time.
fallback: Use the 10-heading template in the SharePoint folder.
l_obj: Select the 3 must-know messages and a pre-workshop ask.
explain: The pre-read should prepare people to think, not ask them to study.

exercise.situation: You have six slides and ten minutes of attention, seven days before the workshop.
questions: What are the three things they must know?
What do you leave out, and why?
What do you ask them to do before arriving?

answer_key.sample_answer: Who we design for, the moment that hurts most, the question we will work on. Leave out methods and solutions. Ask for one personal story.
answer_key.success_criteria: 3 messages are about users and the challenge; the ask is concrete.

name: Mini Podcast
obj: Turn the approved pre-read into a short two-voice audio story that makes users and tensions memorable.
who: CoDesign team scripts and reviews · Recording by team or approved audio tool.
acc: CoDesign lead reviews accuracy and confidentiality before sharing.
inputs: Approved pre-read only. Minimum evidence: every statement traceable to the pre-read; quotes cleared under sharing rules.
steps: Include user stories and cleared quotes
output: A 5-8 minute podcast (target 6 min, ≤900 spoken words) ending with the questions for co-creation.
std: Word count and duration recorded; nothing beyond the pre-read; no exercise answers.
mistakes: Adding findings not in the pre-read · reconstructed quotes · labelling a script as audio.
handoff: Podcast + pre-read sent; participants arrive with stories.
example: LEARN: two hosts walk through Leila's 3-hour gap, play a cleared paraphrase, and end with 'Bring one place on campus where you wish you could stay'. [fictional]

var.HEAL: Open on Ruth asking 'did he eat?'

prompt: Generic Claude prompt: 'Using only this approved pre-read [paste], write a two-voice script of max 900 words in 6 timed sections: opening tension, why this session, essential context, what the evidence says, unresolved tensions, what to bring. Mark pauses. Do not add facts or reveal exercises.'
verify: Line-by-line check against pre-read; quotes attribution; word count.
fallback: Record a 5-minute voice memo reading the pre-read story with two voices.
l_obj: Choose an opening story and protect confidentiality while keeping the human voice.
explain: Don't make participants listen to a report. Make them experience the story behind the research.

templates.label: Pre-read J-7 folder (podcast script template: MISSING, owner Gabriel)

exercise.situation: Turn twelve interviews into a six-minute audio story.
questions: Which user story do you open with, and why?
How do you protect confidentiality but keep quotes alive?
Which question do you leave the listener with?

answer_key.sample_answer: Open with the most typical, not the most extreme, story. Paraphrase or use cleared quotes with role, not name. End with the workshop question.
answer_key.success_criteria: Opening story is representative; no identifiable person.

name: Ice Breaker — Preparation
obj: Design a short activity that creates a safe, collaborative and user-focused mood for the workshop.
when: Designed in Define; run at the start of Co-create (05.02).
inputs: Participant list, workshop objective, persona. Minimum: group size and mix known.
output: A ready-to-run ice breaker card: objective, duration, group size, materials, instructions, prompt, tips, transition.
std: 5-10 minutes; everyone contributes; ends on the challenge.
mistakes: Games unrelated to the topic · activities that embarrass people · no transition.
example: PLAY: 'My best and worst half-time' — each person writes one of each on two stickies in 2 minutes; the facilitator clusters them live and says 'this is what Dev lives every match'.

var.WORK: 'The best lunch I had with my team' story in 60 seconds.
var.HEAL: 'A meal someone cared about' — avoid personal medical stories.
var.LEARN: 'Where I hid on campus between classes.'

prompt: Generic Claude prompt: 'Propose 3 seven-minute ice breakers for [group mix] on [challenge] that activate [behaviour]. Each with instructions, prompt and transition to the first activity.'
verify: Inclusive, accessible, culturally appropriate for the US audience.
fallback: Default: 'one word for how users feel at [moment]' round.
l_obj: Design a 7-minute ice breaker that activates a named behaviour and transitions to the first activity.
explain: The best ice breaker already starts the workshop.

templates.label: Project template root (SharePoint) — ice breaker card: TO CREATE, owner Diane

exercise.situation: Your workshop mixes a site manager, two dietitians, a CFO and three end users.
questions: Which behaviour do you need to activate first?
Design a seven-minute activity.
How do you connect it to the first real activity?

answer_key.sample_answer: Equal voice and user focus. Silent writing first, then round-robin. Transition: 'These stories are the journey we'll map now.'
answer_key.success_criteria: Behaviour named; silent-first design; explicit transition.
